::: {.lead}
A delivery drone waits at the depot. The player taps on the compass and
chooses "fly at 30°". The game must now move the drone: so many units along
x and so many along y, in every frame. How does it turn an angle into a
movement, and back again? The answer is **trigonometry**: sine, cosine and
tangent. In Lectures 1 to 3 you described directions with vectors. In this
lesson you describe them with an angle, and you change between the two. You
meet the right triangle and the **unit circle**, and then you use them for
motion: the angle to a target, an orb that circles a hero, and a coin that
bobs up and down. Every section ends with a short task. Seminar 4 practises
all of it in game motion problems.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary angle degree right-triangle hypotenuse sine cosine tangent unit-circle quadrant atan2 angular-speed oscillation amplitude period >}}

## 4.1 Which way is the drone facing? Angles

The compass in the corner of the screen shows the heading of the drone:
"90°". Which way is that? Games need one rule for angles, so that 90°
means the same direction for the artist, the designer and the code.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.1 — Angle of a direction"}
The **angle** of a direction is the amount of turn from the positive
x-axis to that direction. It is measured in **degrees** (°). A full turn is
360°. A positive angle turns **anticlockwise**; a negative angle turns
clockwise.
:::

So 0° points along +x (to the right), 90° along +y (up), 180° along −x and
270° along −y (@fig-dial). Unity uses the same rule for the rotation of a 2D
object around z: a positive angle turns it anticlockwise.

![Angles in game maths. A negative angle turns clockwise: −45° is the same direction as 315°.](images/angle-dial.png){#fig-dial width=92%}

Two angles show the same direction when they differ by a full turn:
370° = 370° − 360° = 10°, and −90° = −90° + 360° = 270°.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.1 — The four main directions"}
1. A drone with the heading 0° flies to the right (+x).
2. With 90° it flies up (+y); with 180° to the left (−x).
3. With 270° it flies down (−y). The same heading is also written −90°.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.2 — Turning past a full turn"}
A turret faces 350°. It turns 20° anticlockwise.

1. The new angle is 350° + 20° = 370°.
2. 370° − 360° = 10°. The turret faces 10°, a little above +x.
3. Another turret faces 0° and turns 45° clockwise: 0° − 45° = −45°, the
   same as 315°.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using the compass of a map. On a map, 0° is north (up) and angles turn
clockwise. In game maths, 0° is +x (right) and angles turn anticlockwise.
A map heading of 90° (east) is 0° in game maths.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Draw five headings"}
On squared paper, draw the x-axis and the y-axis.

1. Draw an arrow from the origin for 0°, 90°, 135°, 225° and −45°. For 45°
   angles, follow the diagonal of the squares.
2. Write the second name of each angle: for example 270° is also −90°.

*Your result:* the drawing with five labelled arrows.

::: {.check}
0° right, 90° up, 135° up-left on the diagonal, 225° down-left on the
diagonal, −45° down-right on the diagonal. Second names: 0° = 360°,
90° = −270°, 135° = −225°, 225° = −135°, −45° = 315°.
:::
:::

## 4.2 How high is the ramp? Sine, cosine and tangent

A skate game has a ramp that is 10 m long and rises at 30°. The level
designer must know two numbers: how high the ramp goes, and how far forward
it reaches. The ramp, the floor and the height make a **right triangle**:
a triangle with one angle of 90° (@fig-tri).

For one angle θ (the Greek letter "theta") of a right triangle, the three
sides have names:

- the **hypotenuse**: the longest side, opposite the right angle (the ramp);
- the **opposite** side: across from θ (the height);
- the **adjacent** side: next to θ, but not the hypotenuse (the floor).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.2 — Sine, cosine and tangent"}
For an angle θ of a right triangle:
$$\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}.$$
:::

![The ramp as a right triangle. With the hypotenuse 10 and θ = 30°, the height is 5 and the floor part is 8.7.](images/right-triangle.png){#fig-tri width=94%}

The three values depend only on the angle, not on the size of the
triangle. A calculator gives them; for the angles that games use most, learn
@tbl-trig (values to two decimals).

| θ | 0° | 30° | 45° | 60° | 90° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sin θ | 0 | 0.5 | 0.71 | 0.87 | 1 |
| cos θ | 1 | 0.87 | 0.71 | 0.5 | 0 |
| tan θ | 0 | 0.58 | 1 | 1.73 | — |

: Sine, cosine and tangent of the common angles. At 90°, tan does not exist. {#tbl-trig}

From the definition, each side follows from the hypotenuse:
opposite = hypotenuse × sin θ, and adjacent = hypotenuse × cos θ.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.3 — The skate ramp"}
The ramp is 10 m long and rises at 30°. How high is it, and how far forward
does it reach?

1. Height (opposite) = 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = **5 m**.
2. Forward (adjacent) = 10 × cos 30° = 10 × 0.87 = **8.7 m**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.4 — A hill in a racing game"}
A hill rises 3 m over 4 m forward. The slope itself is 5 m long (3, 4, 5:
Lecture 2).

1. sin θ = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6 and cos θ = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.
2. tan θ = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. The tangent is the **slope**: 0.75 m up for every
   1 m forward.
3. 0.75 is between tan 30° = 0.58 and tan 45° = 1, so the hill rises at an
   angle between 30° and 45°.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Mixing up the opposite and the adjacent side. They depend on the angle you
look from. For the other sharp angle of the ramp (60°, at the top), the
height is the *adjacent* side.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The calculator of your phone"}
Open the calculator of your phone or of the lab computer in scientific mode
(Android: tap the arrow or turn the phone; iPhone: turn the phone, or choose
Scientific; Windows: the menu → Scientific). Check that it shows **DEG**,
not RAD.

1. Compute sin 30°, cos 30° and tan 45°. Compare with @tbl-trig.
2. A ramp is 10 m long and rises at 20°. Compute its height: 10 × sin 20°.

*Your result:* three values and the height of the ramp.

::: {.check}
sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87, tan 45° = 1, as in @tbl-trig. The ramp:
10 × sin 20° ≈ 10 × 0.34 = 3.4 m. If you got −0.99 for sin 30, the calculator
is in RAD mode.
:::
:::

## 4.3 Every angle at once: the unit circle

The drone can fly at 120° or 250° too. But a right triangle has no angle
bigger than 90°. The **unit circle** gives sine and cosine for *every*
angle (@fig-unit).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.3 — The unit circle"}
The **unit circle** is the circle with the radius 1 around the origin. The
point on it at the angle θ is
$$(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta).$$
So cos θ is the x-coordinate of the point, and sin θ is its y-coordinate.
:::

For angles from 0° to 90°, this is the triangle of section 4.2 with the
hypotenuse 1. For larger angles, the same numbers come back, but with signs:
on the left side of the circle x is negative, below the x-axis y is
negative.

![The unit circle. The points at 30°, 150°, 210° and 330° have the same numbers with different signs.](images/unit-circle.png){#fig-unit width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.5 — The four main directions"}
1. 0°: the point (1, 0), so cos 0° = 1 and sin 0° = 0.
2. 90°: (0, 1). 180°: (−1, 0). 270°: (0, −1).
3. At 90° and 270° cos θ = 0. So tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ does not exist there.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.6 — Mirror angles"}
At 30° the point is (0.87, 0.5) (@fig-unit).

1. 150° is the mirror image across the y-axis: (−0.87, 0.5).
2. 210° is half a turn from 30°: (−0.87, −0.5).
3. 330° is the mirror image across the x-axis: (0.87, −0.5).
:::

Every point of the unit circle is 1 unit from the origin. With the
Pythagorean theorem (Lecture 2): $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$. For
example $0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1$. So **(cos θ, sin θ) is always a
unit vector**.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing the point as (sin θ, cos θ). The x-coordinate comes first, and it is
the **cosine**. At 90° the point is (0, 1), not (1, 0).
:::

{{< sim file="sims/unit-circle-lab.html" poster="sims/unit-circle-lab.png" title="Unit Circle Lab: cos, sin and tan for every angle" height="720" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Four points in Unit Circle Lab"}
Open the **Unit Circle Lab** simulator above (or scan its QR code).

1. Put the point at 30°, 150°, 210° and 330°.
2. Each time, write cos θ and sin θ.

*Your result:* a table with four rows, and one sentence: what changes from
one row to the next, and what stays the same?

::: {.check}
30°: (0.87, 0.5); 150°: (−0.87, 0.5); 210°: (−0.87, −0.5); 330°:
(0.87, −0.5). The numbers stay the same; only the signs change with the
quadrant.
:::
:::

## 4.4 From an angle to a movement

The player sets the heading of the drone to 30° and the speed to 10 units
per second. In Lecture 2 you learned: velocity = direction × speed, where
the direction is a unit vector. The unit circle gives this unit vector
directly: it is (cos θ, sin θ).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.4 — Velocity from an angle"}
An object that moves at the angle θ with the speed s has the velocity
$$\mathbf{v} = s\,(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta) = (s\cos\theta,\ s\sin\theta).$$
:::

![The drone flies at 30° with the speed 10: 8.7 units along x and 5 along y in one second.](images/angle-velocity.png){#fig-vel width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.7 — The drone at 30°"}
The heading is 30°, and the speed is 10 (@fig-vel).

1. The direction is (cos 30°, sin 30°) = (0.87, 0.5).
2. The velocity is 10 × (0.87, 0.5) = **(8.7, 5)** units per second.
3. After 1 second the drone is at (8.7, 5); after 2 seconds at (17.4, 10).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.8 — A ball kicked backwards"}
A ball is kicked at 135° with the speed 4.

1. 135° is in the second quadrant: x negative, y positive. The direction is
   (cos 135°, sin 135°) = (−0.71, 0.71).
2. The velocity is 4 × (−0.71, 0.71) = (−2.84, 2.84), about **(−2.8, 2.8)**.
3. The ball moves to the left and up, at the same speed in both parts.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Multiplying the speed by the angle: "10 × 30 = 300". The angle only chooses
the direction. Multiply the speed by cos θ and by sin θ.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Velocity from the unit circle"}
A boat sails at 60° with the speed 6.

1. In **Unit Circle Lab**, put the point at 60°. Read cos 60° and sin 60°.
2. Multiply both by 6 on paper. Check the length of your vector with the
   Pythagorean theorem: is it about 6?

*Your result:* the velocity of the boat and your check.

::: {.check}
cos 60° = 0.5 and sin 60° ≈ 0.87: velocity 6 × (0.5, 0.87) ≈ (3, 5.2).
Check: 3² + 5.2² ≈ 9 + 27 = 36 = 6².
:::
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
Game code measures angles in **radians**, another unit for angles. So it
turns degrees into radians first with `Mathf.Deg2Rad`:

```csharp
float angle = 30 * Mathf.Deg2Rad;                    // 30° in radians
Vector2 dir = new Vector2(Mathf.Cos(angle), Mathf.Sin(angle));
Vector2 velocity = 10 * dir;                         // (8.7, 5)
```
Without `* Mathf.Deg2Rad`, `Mathf.Sin(30)` would read 30 as radians and give
a wrong value (−0.99).
:::

## 4.5 Which angle is the target at?

A turret stands at the origin. A drone hovers at $(4, 4)$. To turn the
turret, the game needs the *angle* of the drone, not only the vector
$\mathbf{d} = (4, 4)$ to it. In section 4.4 you went from an angle to a
direction. Now you go back: from a direction to an angle.

The tangent helps first: $\tan\theta = d_y \div d_x = 4 \div 4 = 1$, and
tan 45° = 1, so the drone is at 45°. But there is a problem (@fig-atan2).
A drone at $(-4, -4)$ gives $(-4) \div (-4) = 1$ too. Yet it is behind the
turret, at −135°. The division loses the signs.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.5 — atan2"}
**atan2(y, x)** gives the angle of the vector $(x, y)$ from the positive
x-axis. It looks at the signs of both parts, so it gives the right angle in
every quadrant, from −180° to 180°.
:::

![A and C have the same slope, but not the same angle. atan2 uses the signs of x and y.](images/atan2.png){#fig-atan2 width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.9 — Four drones"}
The turret is at (0, 0).

1. A at $(4, 4)$: atan2(4, 4) = **45°**.
2. B at $(-4, 4)$: atan2(4, −4) = **135°**. tan alone would say −45°.
3. C at $(-4, -4)$: atan2(−4, −4) = **−135°** (the same direction as 225°).
4. E at $(0, -3)$: straight down, atan2(−3, 0) = **−90°**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Swapping the order. atan2 takes **y first**: atan2(y, x). With x first, a
drone at $(4, 0)$ comes out at 90° instead of 0°.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Angles on paper"}
On squared paper, mark a turret at the origin and the targets $(5, 0)$,
$(0, 4)$, $(-3, 3)$ and $(-3, -3)$.

1. Draw the vector $\mathbf{d}$ to each target and name its quadrant.
2. Write the angle that atan2 gives. Use the axes and the 45° diagonals.

*Your result:* a table with four rows: the vector, the quadrant and the
angle.

::: {.check}
$(5, 0)$: 0° (on the x-axis). $(0, 4)$: 90° (on the y-axis). $(-3, 3)$:
135° (quadrant II). $(-3, -3)$: −135°, the same as 225° (quadrant III).
:::
:::

## 4.6 Moving in a circle

A magic orb circles the hero to protect her. A moon goes around a planet. A
saw blade spins around a pole. All of them move in a circle at a steady
speed. The unit circle of section 4.3 gives the position: the point at the
angle θ on a circle with the radius r around the centre C is
$C + r(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ (@fig-orbit).

The angle grows at a steady rate. This rate is the **angular speed** ω (the
Greek letter "omega"), in degrees per second:
$$\theta = \omega \times t.$$

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.6 — Circular motion"}
An object that moves in a circle with the centre C and the radius r, at the
angular speed ω, starting at 0°, is at
$$P(t) = C + r\,(\cos(\omega t),\ \sin(\omega t)).$$
One full turn takes the **period** $T = 360° \div \omega$.
:::

![The orb circles C = (5, 5) with the radius 2, at 90° per second.](images/orbit.png){#fig-orbit width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.10 — The orb"}
C = (5, 5), r = 2, ω = 90° per second.

1. t = 0: θ = 0°, $P = (5, 5) + 2 \times (1, 0) = (7, 5)$.
2. t = 1 s: θ = 90°, $P = (5, 5) + 2 \times (0, 1) = (5, 7)$.
3. t = 2 s: θ = 180°, $P = (3, 5)$; t = 3 s: θ = 270°, $P = (5, 3)$.
4. The period is 360° ÷ 90° = **4 s**: at t = 4 s the orb is back at (7, 5).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Forgetting the radius or the centre. (cos θ, sin θ) is on a circle of
radius 1 around (0, 0). Multiply by r, then add C.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/wave-lab.html" poster="sims/wave-lab.png" title="Wave Lab: circle, bob and sweep" height="760" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · An orbit in Wave Lab"}
Open the **Wave Lab** simulator above. Choose the mode **Orbit**, the
amplitude 2 (the radius) and the period 4 s.

1. Step to 0 s, 1 s, 2 s and 3 s. Write the position each time.
2. Change the period to 8 s. What is the angular speed now?

*Your result:* four positions and the new angular speed.

::: {.check}
Wave Lab circles the centre (0, 2): 0 s: (2, 2); 1 s: (0, 4); 2 s: (−2, 2);
3 s: (0, 0). Period 8 s: ω = 360° ÷ 8 = 45° per second.
:::
:::

## 4.7 Bobbing up and down: oscillating motion

A coin floats in the air and bobs gently, so that the player notices it. A
lift goes up and down beside a cliff. Such motion goes back and forth around
a middle position and repeats: an **oscillation**. Look at the orb of
section 4.6 from the side: its height goes up and down. Its height is the
sine of the angle. So the sine gives the bobbing (@fig-wave):

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.7 — Oscillation with sine"}
A value that bobs around the middle c, with the **amplitude** A and the
**period** T, is
$$y(t) = c + A\sin\!\left(360° \times \frac{t}{T}\right).$$
A is the largest distance from the middle. T is the time of one full up and
down.
:::

![A bobbing value: middle 2, amplitude 3, period 4 s. It is at the top at 1 s and at the bottom at 3 s.](images/sine-wave.png){#fig-wave width=94%}

At a quarter of the period, the angle is 90° and sin = 1: the top, c + A.
At three quarters, the angle is 270° and sin = −1: the bottom, c − A. At 0,
half and the full period, sin = 0: the middle.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.11 — A bobbing coin"}
A coin has the middle 4, the amplitude 1 and the period 2 s:
$y(t) = 4 + 1 \times \sin(360° \times t \div 2)$.

1. t = 0: sin 0° = 0, y = 4 (the middle).
2. t = 0.5 s: the angle is 360° × 0.5 ÷ 2 = 90°, y = 4 + 1 = **5** (the top).
3. t = 1.5 s: the angle is 270°, y = 4 − 1 = **3** (the bottom).
4. The coin moves between 3 and 5: 2 units from bottom to top, which is
   2 × A.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading the amplitude as the whole movement. With A = 3, a value moves from
c − 3 to c + 3: 6 units from bottom to top, twice the amplitude.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The lift in Wave Lab"}
In **Wave Lab**, choose the mode **Bob**, the amplitude 3 and the period 4 s.

1. Step to 0 s, 1 s, 2 s, 3 s and 4 s. Write the height each time.
2. Change the period to 8 s. When is the lift at the top now?

*Your result:* five heights and the new time of the top.

::: {.check}
The middle is 2: 0 s: 2; 1 s: 5; 2 s: 2; 3 s: −1; 4 s: 2. With the period
8 s the top comes at a quarter of it: 2 s.
:::
:::

### Sweeping back and forth

The same sine can make an *angle* swing. In a stealth game, a searchlight on a tower sweeps the yard: left, right,
left. Here the *angle* oscillates, not the height. The tower faces +x, and
its light swings 45° to each side, with the period 4 s (@fig-sweep):
$$\text{angle}(t) = 45° \times \sin(360° \times t \div 4).$$
At each moment, the beam points in the direction
(cos angle, sin angle), as in section 4.4.

![A searchlight sweeps from −45° to 45° and back in 4 seconds.](images/searchlight.png){#fig-sweep width=92%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.12 — The searchlight"}
1. t = 0: angle 0°, the beam points along (1, 0).
2. t = 1 s: angle 45° × sin 90° = 45°; the beam points along
   (0.71, 0.71).
3. t = 3 s: angle 45° × sin 270° = −45°; the beam points along
   (0.71, −0.71).
4. It covers 90° in all: 45° to each side.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Mixing up the two oscillations. For the lift the *position* bobs; for the
searchlight the *angle* swings, and the beam still starts at the tower. Use the angle
to make the direction (cos, sin).
:::

## Case study: Drone Drop

*Drone Drop* is a made-up delivery game. The depot is at (0, 0). The drone
always flies at the speed 10 units per second, for exactly 1 second, and
then drops the parcel. The player only chooses the heading. Three customers
wait: Ana at (5, 8.7), Ben at (0, 10) and Cara at (−7.1, 7.1). Each house is
10 units from the depot, so each heading must point straight at a house.
The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these numbers. In the
mini-game below you deliver five parcels.

{{< sim file="sims/drone-drop.html" poster="sims/drone-drop.png" title="Drone Drop: choose the heading to each house" kind="game" height="780" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 1 (trigonometry: the trig functions, the unit circle and
atan2) and Chapter 8 (orientation in 2D as an angle).

## Exercises

1. Which direction is 180°? And −90°?
2. A ramp is 8 m long and rises at 30°. How high is it?
3. A ladder is 10 m long and leans at 60° to the floor. How far is its foot from the wall?
4. A hill rises 6 m over 8 m forward. Find sin θ, cos θ and tan θ.
5. What are the coordinates of the point at 90° on the unit circle? At 180°?
6. The point at 60° is (0.5, 0.87). Write the points at 120°, 240° and 300°.
7. A car drives at 0° with the speed 12. What is its velocity?
8. A drone flies at 45° with the speed 10. What is its velocity?
9. Find the angle of the vectors $(5, 5)$, $(-5, 5)$ and $(0, -2)$ with atan2.
10. An orb circles $C = (2, 3)$ with the radius 3, at 90° per second, starting at 0°. Where is it at 1 s and at 2 s?
11. A moon circles $(0, 0)$ with the radius 6, at 45° per second. What is its period?
12. $y = 1 + 2\sin(360° \times t \div 8)$. Find y at 0 s, 2 s, 4 s and 6 s.
13. A coin bobs between 3 and 5. What are its middle and its amplitude?
14. A lift has the period 6 s. When is it at the top for the first time?
15. A searchlight sweeps with angle = 30° × sin(360° × t ÷ 4). What is the angle at 1 s, and in which direction does the beam point then?
16. *Drone Drop*: which heading reaches Cara at (−7.1, 7.1)? Where does the parcel fall with the heading 210°?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 180°: to the left (−x). −90°: down (−y), the same as 270°.
2. 8 × sin 30° = 8 × 0.5 = 4 m.
3. The floor part is adjacent: 10 × cos 60° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m.
4. The slope is 10 m (6, 8, 10). sin θ = 0.6, cos θ = 0.8, tan θ = 0.75.
5. (0, 1) and (−1, 0).
6. 120°: (−0.5, 0.87); 240°: (−0.5, −0.87); 300°: (0.5, −0.87).
7. 12 × (1, 0) = (12, 0).
8. 10 × (0.71, 0.71) = (7.1, 7.1).
9. 45°, 135° and −90°.
10. 1 s: (2, 3) + 3 × (0, 1) = (2, 6). 2 s: (2, 3) + 3 × (−1, 0) = (−1, 3).
11. 360° ÷ 45° = 8 s.
12. 1, 3, 1, −1 (the angles are 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°).
13. Middle 4, amplitude 1.
14. At a quarter of the period: 1.5 s.
15. 30° × sin 90° = 30°; the beam points along (0.87, 0.5).
16. 135°. 210° gives 10 × (−0.87, −0.5) = (−8.7, −5): no house is there.
:::
